title: Bowed bass solos as a novelty; Slim and Slam ends in 1941
summary: Bowing was almost unheard of in jazz bass then; Stewart popularized bowed solos and bassists like John Kirby were fascinated. The duo lasted until Slim was drafted in 1941.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now, were many, like I know I've heard like there are a few things Duke Ellington had in the early
which he used Braud for '30s before (inaudible) on bow.
But there wasn't much, to my knowledge, there wasn't much bowing going on with jazz bass players at that time.

No, there wasn't very much. At times on slow numbers there was, they would bow straight notes, you know, not solo-wise. They would just be bowing the fundamental bass notes, you know, to the music, of course, whatever they were playing. And that's about the only time they would be bowing, which was very little.
So that to a certain extent you kind of began to popularize amongst bass players or make people notice the possibility of bowing.
Yeah, soloing with the bow, yeah.
Uh-huh. And now like did you -- did you -- did many of the bass players around at that time, like say Braud or John Kirby or any of those guys, did they take interest in what you were doing?

Yes, very much. I used to -- oh, whenever I would visit another group, like John Kirby asked me to come up and play, and that's when I did my thing, of course, you know, and quite a few bass players were very interested in
that bowing. They were -- they thought it was fascinating, you know.
So now, you -- you were in this -- so like, how long did the band -- so like when you all started, Slim and Slam, that was 1935. How long did that band exist?
Yeah. When Slim had to go in the service, he had to -- he was inducted into the Army, and that's when that ended.
